explanation:
## How the puzzle works

**What the grid contains.** Every input is a black (0) canvas holding a few isolated single pixels. Each pixel is a 1×1 object.

**What changes.** In every output, each pixel gets a 3×3 square ring around it, made of the 8 neighbours. The pixel itself stays the same. The ring's colour depends only on the pixel's colour, and the demonstrations agree on it every time:

| pixel colour | ring colour | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 6 | pairs 1, 2, 4 |
| 8 | 4 | pairs 3, 4 |
| 2 | 1 | pairs 1, 4 |

There is no obvious arithmetic link between the two colours, so I treat this as a lookup table (a legend).

**Edges and neighbours.**
- In pair 2 the 3 sits on row 1, so its ring reaches row 0. In pair 4 the 3 sits at column 1, so its ring reaches column 0. In both cases the ring fits exactly on the grid. To be safe, the program still clips any ring cell that would fall outside the grid.
- In pair 4 the rings of 8 and 2 touch diagonally but never overlap. To be safe, the program only paints cells that are still background, so it never covers an original pixel or another ring.

**Checking against the demonstrations.** The fact sheet lists the changed cells of each pair. Each one is exactly one of the 8 neighbours of a seed pixel, painted with the mapped colour. Every pair changes exactly 8 cells per seed (8, 8, 8 and 24), which matches a complete ring with no clipping or overlap.

**Applying it to the test.** The test has three pixels, and all three colours appear in the table:
- 3 at (1,1) → ring of 6 covering rows 0–2, columns 0–2.
- 2 at (10,13) → ring of 1 covering rows 9–11, columns 12–14.
- 8 at (14,2) → ring of 4 covering rows 13–15, columns 1–3.

All three rings fit inside the 16×16 grid without overlapping.

**Construction stages.** The program starts from a copy of the input. It stamps one ring per seed pixel, in reading order, and emits the canvas after each ring. Finally it emits and returns the finished grid.
